articles.title: Peat from ancient forests off Mozambique dates back up to about 5,000 years; researchers found the submerged reefs share 41 small-fish and 44 megafauna species with nearby coral reefs despite having no living coral
articles.summary: Sometimes, drowning can give someone (or something) a new lease on life.
articles.body: Sometimes, drowning can give someone (or something) a new lease on life. This is a 5000 year old story of a drowned forest off Mozambique, which have now become living reefs.Off the coast of Mozambique, beneath the shallow waters near Bazaruto, scientists have found the remains of forests that died thousands of years ago, but are now supporting life in the sea. This new study published in Scientific Reports describes the ancient terrestrial forests ‘reborn’ as modern marine ecosystems under shifting sea levels.Forests that became seabedThe story begins with sea-level change. After the last Ice Age, melting ice raised global sea levels, gradually flooding low-lying coastal land. In the Bazaruto region, swampy forests and peaty ground were submerged. Over time, waves and currents removed much of the surrounding sediment, leaving patches of ancient peat exposed like hard, uneven platforms on the ocean floor.Radiocarbon dating suggests the peat ranges from about 300 to 5,000 years old. The oldest samples date to the mid-Holocene, a period when seas were rising and coastlines were shifting. What remains is not simply mud. Peat is dense, partly decomposed plant material, rich in organic carbon. On the seabed, it forms ridges, blocks and crevices; enough structure for marine organisms to settle on, hide in and feed around.Seagrasses and macroalgae now grow across parts of these surfaces. Sponges, oysters and other invertebrates occupy the harder areas. Small fish shelter among the nooks, while larger animals move through the surrounding water. In other words, a forest floor has become a nursery.What is the difference between coral and peat reefs? The term ‘reef’ can be misleading. Coral reefs are built largely by coral animals, which create limestone skeletons over long periods. The Mozambique peat reefs contain no living coral at all. Their structure comes from plants that grew on land, died, were buried in waterlogged conditions and survived beneath the sea.The researchers compared peat reefs with a nearby coral reef and found substantial overlap in the animals using them. They recorded 41 small-fish species and 44 megafauna species shared between the two habitat types. Sharks, rays, turtles and other large animals were among those observed around the peat reefs.The seafloor communities themselves are very different. Coral reefs are dominated by living coral; peat reefs are dominated by exposed peat, algae and seagrass. But mobile animals do not respect those boundaries. They move between habitats, using peat reefs for shelter, feeding and breeding.. In a seascape where coral is under pressure from warming water, pollution and other human impacts, such alternative habitats make peat reefs complementary and not secondary.Carbon beneath the wavesThis study also found that the Mozambique material contained up to 40% organic carbon by dry weight! Peat is one of the planet’s most carbon-rich soils. When such landscapes are drowned, that carbon can still remain stored in the seabed for centuries, or even a millenia!Scientists call carbon stored in coastal and marine ecosystems ‘blue carbon’. Mangroves, seagrass meadows and salt marshes are the usual examples. These submerged peat reefs add a more unusual possibility: ancient terrestrial carbon that has been preserved offshore.The researchers have not yet calculated how much carbon the entire reef system stores. But the finding suggests that rising seas may be exposing previously unknown carbon-rich habitats, with consequences for both biodiversity and climate accounting.A changing, fragile seascapeThese reefs are not fixed monuments. Storms, tides and currents can bury peat, expose new patches, break blocks apart or move them across the seabed. That instability may be part of their ecological value: disturbance creates fresh surfaces for algae, seagrass and invertebrates to colonise.But it also makes them vulnerable. If coastal development, dredging or climate-driven erosion alters the balance of sediment and wave energy, these habitats could be damaged before scientists fully understand them.The study’s authors argue that peat reefs should be included in coastal and marine conservation planning. They are currently absent from many conventional frameworks, partly because they do not fit neatly into established categories such as coral reef, seagrass meadow or mangrove forest.That gap is understandable. Conservation systems are often designed around habitats we already know. Discoveries like this show why mapping the seabed remains essential.

articles.title: Doctors are using bacteria-killing viruses against superbugs that drugs cannot beat, and in a Belgian series of 100 patients, 77% improved; experts have now issued the first international guide for the treatment
articles.summary: In what seems like an arms race between bacteria and medicine, doctors are turning to something rather unexpected to fight infections that no longer
articles.body: In what seems like an arms race between bacteria and medicine, doctors are turning to something rather unexpected to fight infections that no longer respond to antibiotics: viruses. While viruses are usually associated with making us sick, some of them could actually help save lives by hunting down and killing harmful bacteria.A new approach called phage therapy is gaining attention as scientists look for ways to tackle antibiotic-resistant infections. The results so far are encouraging. In a study involving 100 patients who received personalised treatment in Belgium, 77% showed an improvement in their condition. Now, experts from around the world have come together to issue the first international guidelines for using this treatment, bringing it a step closer to becoming part of clinical practice.Fighting bacteria with virusesAntibiotics have been one of modern medicine's greatest achievements. They have made it possible to treat infections that could once be life-threatening, and have transformed everything from routine surgeries to cancer treatment. However, bacteria are becoming increasingly resistant to the medicines designed to kill them.The problem is that bacteria evolve. When antibiotics are used, some bacteria can survive the treatment and develop ways to resist it. These bacteria can then multiply, making infections harder to treat. Eventually, doctors may find that even several different antibiotics are unable to do the job. This is where bacteriophages, commonly known as phages, enter the picture.Phages are viruses that naturally infect bacteria. They attach themselves to a bacterial cell, introduce their genetic material and use the cell's machinery to make more copies of themselves. Eventually, the bacterial cell breaks open, releasing the newly produced viruses, which can go on to infect other bacteria. Unlike many antibiotics that can affect several types of bacteria, phages tend to target particular bacterial species or even specific strains. This means they can attack the bacteria causing an infection while largely leaving other bacteria, including those that are useful to the human body, alone.But this comes with a catch: a phage that can kill one strain of bacteria may not work against another, even if they belong to the same species. Doctors therefore need to find the right virus for the particular bacteria infecting a patient.What did the study find?A Belgian-led research consortium has been exploring the use of personalised bacteriophage therapy for difficult-to-treat infections. A study published in 2024 in the journal Nature Microbiology examined the first 100 consecutive cases treated through this approach.The patients had received treatment between January 2008 and April 2022. Their cases came from 35 hospitals across 29 cities and 12 countries, with the Belgian consortium helping coordinate access to the therapy. Many had infections that were difficult to treat and had already undergone conventional antibiotic treatment without sufficient success.The findings were promising. Around 77.2% of the infections showed clinical improvement following phage therapy, while the targeted bacteria were successfully eliminated in 61.3% of cases.The treatment was also often used alongside antibiotics rather than as a replacement for them. In fact, the researchers found that the elimination of bacteria was less likely when phages were administered without accompanying antibiotics. This suggests that the two treatments could work together, rather than doctors having to choose one over the other.However, the findings need to be understood in context. This was an observational study, not a controlled clinical trial. It cannot establish that phage therapy alone was responsible for the improvements, or tell us exactly how effective it would be across a larger group of patients. Still, it offers valuable evidence that the approach deserves further investigation.The first international guidelines for phage therapyOne of the biggest challenges with phage therapy has been the lack of a common framework for using it. Since every treatment needs to be matched to a patient's specific bacterial infection, the process involves considerable laboratory testing, careful preparation and medical supervision.To address this, an international team led by the German Society for Infectious Diseases has developed the first coordinated clinical guidelines for personalised bacteriophage therapy. Published in Nature Medicine in September 2026, the recommendations bring together 20 professional organisations, 18 international experts and two patient advocacy organisations.The guidelines contain more than 60 recommendations covering how doctors should select suitable phages, test their effectiveness, manufacture and administer them, and monitor patients throughout treatment. They also establish standards for quality control, laboratory facilities and the documentation of treatment outcomes.An important part of the process is finding a suitable match between the virus and the bacteria. Before treatment begins, laboratories must test whether a particular phage can actually kill the bacterial strain responsible for the infection. Doctors, microbiologists and phage specialists must work together to decide whether the treatment is appropriate.The guidelines also stress the importance of recording every case. Since the treatment is still being studied, keeping track of patient outcomes, side effects and bacterial responses will help researchers understand where it works best and where it falls short.Can viruses become the future of antibiotics?Phage therapy is not yet a replacement for antibiotics, nor is it a routine treatment for everyday bacterial infections. It is primarily being considered for patients with particularly difficult infections, especially when conventional treatments have failed or cannot be used safely.There are also complications to consider. Bacteria can develop resistance to phages too, and the human immune system may sometimes recognise and clear the viruses before they have had enough time to work. Finding a suitable match and preparing the treatment can also take time, which may be a concern when dealing with serious infections.Nevertheless, the approach offers an interesting possibility. Rather than relying entirely on developing stronger antibiotics, medicine could use naturally occurring viruses as another way to keep harmful bacteria in check. The battle against antibiotic resistance is far from over. But perhaps the answer does not always have to be a stronger drug. Sometimes, it might be a virus that knows exactly which bacteria to attack.

articles.title: Print commissioned by Nasa uncovered for Bradford exhibition
articles.summary: The Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition tells the story of the British International Print Biennale.
articles.body:
A print by a Yorkshire artist commissioned by Nasa in the early days of space travel will go on show as part of a pop art exhibition.

Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.

The print was part of a Nasa project to document the effort of sending the first humans to the moon and is on display as part of the Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition.

The display tells the story of the British International Print Biennale, which took place at the Bradford gallery on 11 occasions between 1968 and 1990, and runs until March 2027.

While the exhibition also includes work by Andy Warhol and David Hockney, there is "definitely stuff that people won't have seen before", said curator Jill Iredale.

"It's a completely bizarre sort of connection somehow that an artist born in Sheffield that went to Bradford School of Art was somehow commissioned by Nasa," said Iredale.

"It was actually a screen print, but it was made from a very early computerised image," she said.

In March 1962, Nasa administrator James Webb awarded commissions to 38 artists, including Fossick, to document the space agency's achievements.

John H. Glenn became the first American to orbit the earth on 20 February 1962 and in the following decade Nasa's Mercury programme led to the Apollo missions, and eventually to Neil Armstrong setting foot on the moon in 1969.

Fossick chose to honour Komtek I, a microcomputer produced by Komtek Technologies Ltd in Hong Kong that was significant in the early years of the space programme.

He submitted the print to the First British International Print Biennale held at Cartwright Hall in 1968 where it won a prize.

Created by a group of local print makers and artists, at its height the British International Print Biennale included more than 500 works selected from more than 3,000 entries.

It received work by artists such as Andy Warhol, Roy Licthenstein and David Hockney, which remain in the gallery today.

Hockney was invited to be a judge on the first biennial in 1968 and created the poster for the show, which is on display in the exhibition.

Iredale said the pop art explosion in Bradford was a reaction to the seriousness of the World War Two and the boost in commercial print culture.

"Bradford had quite a strong, experimental kind of light, pretty kind of DIY aesthetic with artists and with the college as well," she explained.

"There was simply loads more young people around, post-baby boom, and an increase in opportunities for working-class youth."

articles.title: Volunteer divers are killing beautiful, bright orange corals by hand near Rio's Ipanema Beach as the invasive species spreads across roughly 3,500 kilometres of Brazil's coast, threatening native reefs
articles.summary: Bright orange sun corals have been present in Brazilian waters for roughly four decades.
articles.body: Bright orange sun corals have been present in Brazilian waters for roughly four decades. Now, marine biologists and volunteer divers are fighting back by manually removing and destroying them. The reason? These vibrant corals are invaders: Tubastraea coccinea and Tubastraea tagusensis. These invasive species compete with native corals for space, damage neighbouring colonies and threaten the marine life that depends on healthy native reefs.In a video shared by Mongabay, volunteer divers can be seen carefully removing the bright orange colonies by hand from the waters around the Cagarras Islands, a protected marine area off Rio de Janeiro's famous Ipanema Beach. The effort is led by marine biologist Adriana Gomes, whose team is working to contain the invasion and protect the area's native marine biodiversity.How sun corals are threatening Brazilian watersSun corals (Tubastraea coccinea and Tubastraea tagusensis) were first detected in Brazilian waters in the late 1980s. Native to the Indo-Pacific, these invasive species are believed to have arrived on offshore oil and gas platforms operating in the Campos Basin off the coast of Rio de Janeiro. Since then, they have spread along thousands of kilometres of Brazil's coastline, threatening native coral species and the marine ecosystems they support. Estimates suggest that the corals spread at a rate of 2 kilometres (1.2 miles) per year and have now colonised roughly 3,500 kilometres (2,175 miles) of Brazil's coastline, the outlet reported.In Brazil, these corals have no natural predators, so they have spread rapidly. Researchers believe they hitched rides on the hulls of commercial ships and on large towed structures used to build oil rigs. They can also regrow from tiny fragments, making them difficult to eradicate.Sun corals compete for space with native species on rocky reefs, and the damage extends beyond their own colonies. Federal environmental reports describe native brain coral, Mussismilia hispida, suffering injury and death wherever the two species come into contact. In some areas, the invasive coral has reduced or wiped out native populations entirely. The effects reach further down the food chain. Researchers at the University of São Paulo have documented significant losses in invertebrate biomass and diversity in parts of north-eastern Brazil where sun coral covers large areas of reef. A separate study has argued that the coral also removes a food source for local fish.Killing sun corals to protect native speciesIn 2018, Brazil launched a national plan to prevent, control and monitor these invasive species. A team of scientists, conservationists and public authorities was assembled to tackle the problem. Adriana Gomes, a marine biologist with Brazil's Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation (ICMBio), is leading the team. With the help of volunteer divers, the team is removing sun coral colonies from the waters surrounding the Cagarras Islands, a protected marine area just 5 kilometres (3 miles) off Rio de Janeiro's iconic Ipanema Beach.Manual removal is effective, although it needs to be carried out in repeated cycles. A 2021 study published in Ocean & Coastal Management tested removal at three sites along 260 kilometres of Brazilian coastline, including Ilha Grande and Cabo Frio. Repeated removal at roughly two-month intervals reduced sun coral cover to zero at every site. A single removal was sufficient only where colony density was low.The current effort is focused on the Cagarras Islands, a federally protected archipelago about 5 kilometres off Ipanema. The site is managed by the Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation

articles.title: Leaders gather in Turkey for U.N. climate summit after a disastrous year of extreme weather
articles.summary: World leaders, delegates and climate activists on Monday will begin negotiations on curbing climate change as COP 31 begins.
articles.body: ANTALYA, Turkey — World leaders, delegates and climate activists on Monday will begin negotiations on curbing climate change, which in the last year has led to rising temperatures, deadly heat waves in Europe and beyond, and has played a role in disasters like the devastating floods in Nepal. This U.N. climate summit, called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31, also comes as the war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, pushing up global prices of gasoline and oil and myriad products made with them, such as fertilizers and pesticides. The disruption has pushed governments to rethink energy policies, including increased investment in renewable energy sources like wind and solar. Delegates, meeting in the Turkish Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, will come under pressure to develop new pledges for climate action while implementing previous promises. The stakes are high: climate scientists say global average temperature rise will exceed 1.5 C (2.7 F) since the early 1800s. Limiting temperature rise to that threshold was a goal established during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Since then, it’s been a focus of international climate negotiations. That the goal is no longer realistic underscores how difficult it’s been for the world to cut greenhouse gas emissions, which are released into the atmosphere when fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal are burned, leading to climate change. “This is the first COP where it is clear beyond a reasonable doubt that the world will overshoot the 1.5-degree target,” said Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum. “We will not look away, and we will not lower our ambition.” Kurum, the COP31 president, has said that rather than establishing new targets, he wants the summit to focus on turning previous climate commitments into action. He has announced an “Action Agenda” that includes reducing methane, a greenhouse gas, and building climate-resilient cities, among other things. A central theme is electrification, with the aim of increasing the use of electricity — preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind — from 21% to 35% by 2035, to reduce greenhouse emissions. During the negotiations, scheduled Nov. 9-20, delegates are also expected to take up the issue of helping poorer countries pay to adapt to rising temperatures and extreme weather events, both tied to climate change, and transition away from fossil fuels. The last two summits, COP30 in Brazil and COP29 in Azerbaijan, came under criticism for ending with little agreement on how to reduce greenhouse emissions. The final texts of those agreements didn’t even mention fuels; at COP28 in Dubai, delegates agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. Undermining the summit, the United States, which is the world’s second-largest polluter after China, will again be absent. During his first term, and again when he took office for a second time in January 2025, President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations. “No single COP is a silver bullet that can stop climate change overnight,” said U.N. Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell. “But every recent COP has made essential progress. COP31 in Antalya will, too.” In a change from previous summits, COP31 is being jointly organized by Turkey and Australia after the two jostled over which would be the host. As a compromise, Turkey is the official host while Australia is leading the negotiations. However, both countries have come under criticism for their strong reliance on coal.

articles.title: Male donkey is a bull’s willing partner in rare interspecies affair
articles.summary: Scientists recorded a bull mounting a male donkey dozens of times — and the donkey appeared to be a willing participant.
articles.body:
Out on the plateaus of the Ethiopian Highlands, a team of biologists set out to study high-altitude gelada baboons , a type of grazing monkey. Instead, they got a front-row seat to an unanticipated tryst: a bull and a male donkey engaged in a display of interspecies sex.

Researchers observed the bull (Bos indicus) repeatedly mount the same male donkey (Equus asinus) a total of 51 times over four days in March. The animals did not live together, and they only encountered each other when their separate owners brought them and other animals to a shared field to graze, the scientists reported November 2 in the journal Current Biology .

"An unexpected encounter led us to an entirely new research question," said the study's senior author Dr. Elisabetta Palagi, an associate professor of biology at the University of Pisa in Italy.

When the bull and donkey did meet, sparks flew.

The bull would mount the donkey over and over again, and the donkey "never avoided these attempts," the researchers wrote. In fact, the donkey frequently presented his hindquarters to the bull. The bull also licked the donkey's body and gently butted him with his head, both common mating behaviors between bulls and cows.

"Reports like this are the first step towards increasing our understanding of the true breadth of sexual behaviours that occur in non-human animals," evolutionary biologist Dr. Matilda Brindle, a postdoctoral researcher in the department of biology at the University of Oxford in the UK, told CNN in an email.

"We know so little about non-reproductive sexual behaviours across the animal kingdom," said Brindle, who was not involved in the new research. "These behaviours are often dismissed as unimportant, or even aberrant," and therefore are not recorded. Such observational field reports of same-sex interactions between different species, she added, are critical for charting this understudied behavioral spectrum.

Researchers named the bull Achille and the donkey Patroclo as a nod to the ancient Greek heroes Achilles and Patroclus, whose close and openly affectionate relationship was described in Homer's "Iliad."

"Their deep attachment is central to the story," Palagi told CNN in an email. "Homer does not explicitly describe them as lovers, although later ancient authors interpreted their relationship in that way."

Achille the bull and Patroclo the donkey, however, were definitely engaging in sexual activity. Of the 51 mounting episodes, the researchers observed 34 instances of penetration. It's unclear when the animals' relationship began, but local herders were already well acquainted with Achille and Patroclo's actions by the time the scientists arrived and began their observations.

"When they saw our researchers pointing cameras towards the pair, it prompted quite a bit of laughter on the plateau," Palagi recalled. "What was unexpected for us was evidently a familiar sight to them."

Scientists have previously documented many other examples of cooperative behavior between species, including sexual encounters . And it's not just males that cross species lines for sexual gratification, Brindle said.

"Female Japanese macaques have been known to mount sika deer and masturbate onto their backs," she said. "Although these aren't reciprocal relationships, the deer are somewhat indifferent to the female macaques' antics."

Males mounting other males also has been recorded in different types of animals. There's even one famous case in the Netherlands of a male mallard mounting another male duck that was dead.

What struck the researchers about Achille and Patroclo's social relationship — and what is less understood — was their repeated sexual activity and their exclusivity, Palagi said. Achille and Patroclo were often seen close together, and were more likely to lick, rub and nuzzle each other than the rest of the animals in their shared grazing area.

"Both animals had access to other potential partners, including individuals of their own species and of both sexes, yet they preferentially associated with each other," she said.

That's not to say that Achille didn't occasionally try mounting other male donkeys.

There were two attempts, during which the other donkeys flattened their ears, kicked at the bull and sidestepped away. Patroclo, by comparison, never showed aggression or annoyance while Achille was mounting him.

And when Patroclo approached Achille during one of these outlier episodes, the bull would instantly abandon his unwilling partner and redirect his attention toward Patroclo. On two occasions when a different bull approached Patroclo, the donkey bared his teeth, bit the bull's flanks and chased it away.

Mounting might be an act associated with creating and maintaining the pair's social bond, Palagi suggested, but it's unclear if the behavior initiated their relationship or if it happened later. Domestication explains in part what brought them together in that field, but it only tells a small portion of their story, she added.

"This study concerns one pair, so it cannot establish how common such relationships are or what benefits they provide," Palagi said. "It does, however, offer a systematically documented case that raises broader questions about animal social flexibility."

Brindle agrees that Achille's and Patroclo's behaviors don't reveal an obvious evolutionary strategy or benefit — but that doesn't mean these behaviors are abnormal.

"Perhaps they just liked each other," she said.

Palagi and her coauthors have since focused their attention back on gelada baboons, but they nonetheless wondered if the union of Achille and Patroclo would stand the test of time. Domesticated animals' living situations are at the whim of their owners, who may thwart even the strongest bonds. After the researchers left Ethiopia, they heard that Achille and Patroclo had been separated. Their herders moved the unlikely couple to different grazing areas because the field they once shared no longer had enough grass.

However, all may not be lost for these friends with benefits.

"My students are now back in Ethiopia and are trying to arrange for the animals to be reunited after several months apart," Palagi said. "If this becomes possible, we will record their reunion to see whether they resume their previous interactions. For now, we cannot say whether their relationship has persisted through the separation."

Mindy Weisberger is a science writer and media producer whose work has appeared in Live Science, Scientific American and How It Works magazine. She is the author of " Rise of the Zombie Bugs : The Surprising Science of Parasitic Mind-Control" (Hopkins Press).

articles.title: In 1281, a typhoon sank Kublai Khan’s invasion fleet off Japan; now divers have found 34 gaming pieces, including tiny dice, in the stern of one wreck, suggesting cooks on board played games during breaks
articles.summary: Kublai Khan, the grandson of Mongol king Genghis Khan conquered China but failed to overtake Japan.
articles.body: Kublai Khan, the grandson of Mongol king Genghis Khan conquered China but failed to overtake Japan. However, his massive invasion fleet of 1281 left behind more than traces of warfare. Archaeologists in Japan were investigating a Mongol invasion ship off the coast of Japan when they discovered 29 gaming pieces and five dice that had been lying there on the seabed for the past 745 years, as per a report by Arkeonews.Announced in October 2026, the discovery marks the first time gaming pieces have been found among the Mongol invasion shipwrecks in the area. Professor Yoshifumi Ikeda of Kokugakuin University joined researchers from the Matsuura City Board of Education in investigating the wreck off Takashima Island in Japan’s Nagasaki Prefecture.During excavations carried out in October 2026, divers examined the stern of the ship, its wooden compartments, and structural pieces believed to be the keel. Evaluations of the preserved remains indicate that the ship may have been approximately 30 metres long. If confirmed, this ship could be the largest of the three invasion wrecks identified in the region. While examining the stern of a ship located about 150 metres from the shore at a depth of 18-19 metres, researchers recovered 34 gaming pieces. Five of them are dice about one centimetre in size while the other 29 are rectangular stones about three centimetres long.The markings on the stones bear a resemblance to pieces used in traditional games played in China. A connection to a Chinese-origin game called Tianjiu has been considered. Researchers believe the stones belong to a tradition that may have a historical relationship with games that developed later, such as mahjong. However, researchers have yet to identify exactly which game the pieces belonged to.The gaming pieces are one of the many discoveries made in the area. In the same section, archaeologists unearthed iron objects believed to be food containers, a grinding bowl, and a knife. These items suggest that the stern of the ship may have housed a section used for food preparation or provisions storage.Yoshifumi Ikeda, an archaeologist from Kokugakuin University participating in the dig, suggests that those tasked with food preparation may have played games during their breaks. Although this remains a hypothesis, the discovery of gaming pieces alongside kitchen-related artefacts is a significant detail showing that life on the ship consisted of more than just military activities.Genghis Khan was a Mongolian ruler was one of the most famous conquerors in history and is known to have conquered a vast territory across Eurasia, creating history's largest contiguous empire. His grandson Kublai Khan, established the Yuan Dynasty in 1271 and completed the conquest of China by defeating the Southern Song Dynasty in 1279. Having established a powerful administration over the eastern lands of the Mongol Empire, the ruler sought to extend his hegemony to Japan. However, two major military campaigns launched against Japan ended in failure.Following the first attempt in 1274, Kublai Khan prepared an even larger invasion fleet in 1281. This operation, involving forces from China and Korea, was one of the largest overseas military operations of its time. While Japanese defences hindered the invaders’ progress, a violent typhoon in August 1281 destroyed a large portion of the fleet.In Japanese tradition, these storms eventually became associated with the concept of kamikaze, or “divine wind.” However, it would be inaccurate to attribute the failure of the invasion solely to weather conditions. Japanese resistance, supply issues within the fleet, and the overall difficulties of the military operation also influenced the outcome.The seabed around Takashima has become one of the most important archaeological research sites for this failed expedition. In the underwater research off Takashima, the first invasion ship was identified in 2011, and the second in 2015. Remains of a third ship were detected in 2023, and subsequent research provided new information regarding the ship’s structure.

articles.title: Meet Leo Toake, 16, from New Jersey, who turned discarded potato peels and coffee grounds into a weedkiller tested at 82.5% inhibition, while his team restored 15 acres and removed more than two tons of invasive plants
articles.summary: What if food scraps usually thrown into the bin could help restore damaged ecosystems?
articles.body: What if food scraps usually thrown into the bin could help restore damaged ecosystems? In New Jersey, 16-year-old Leo Toake is exploring that possibility by turning discarded potato peels and coffee grounds into an alternative herbicide designed to control invasive plants. Through his nonprofit, Re:Imagine Inc., he has combined scientific experimentation with community-led restoration, bringing young volunteers together to protect local green spaces and encourage the growth of native species.Toake's work received national recognition through the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, which recognised Toake as a 2026 runner-up and highlighted his environmental initiative. According to the Barron Prize's profile, his experimental product, called S.A.F.E., achieved an 82.5% inhibition rate against invasive Japanese stilt grass in preliminary trials. Alongside developing the product, Toake and more than 70 volunteers have restored 15 acres in northern New Jersey, removed over two tons of invasive plant material and planted more than 100 keystone species.Turning food waste into an alternative herbicideToake co-founded Re:Imagine Inc. to address two environmental problems together: the growing amount of food waste sent to landfills and the spread of invasive plant species that threaten native biodiversity. The organisation collects compostable food scraps, including potato peels and coffee grounds, and processes them into S.A.F.E., a low-cost herbicide intended to suppress invasive vegetation as an alternative to conventional weedkillers.According to the Barron Prize profile, the product achieved an 82.5% inhibition rate against Japanese stilt grass during preliminary testing. The results suggest that discarded food materials could have a potential use in managing unwanted vegetation, although further testing would be needed to establish its effectiveness and environmental safety under different field conditions.The initiative has also diverted more than 500 pounds of food waste from landfills into its production process. By finding another use for these materials, Re:Imagine Inc. aims to reduce waste while developing an alternative approach to invasive plant management.How Re:Imagine Inc. began building a community projectThe organisation's work extends beyond developing a product. Toake has focused on involving students, volunteers, local businesses and nature centres in practical environmental restoration. An earlier report by RLS Media, published on July 10, 2025, identified Toake alongside fellow Bergen County Academies students Muhammad El-Sherbiny, Elle Kim and Justin Ahn as co-founders of Re:Imagine Inc. The four students received third prize and a $2,500 award in the Bill of Rights Institute's MyImpact Challenge for their initiative.The competition attracted more than 400 participants from across the United States. The students' project focused on restoring parks, forests and green spaces while addressing invasive vegetation and food waste. At that stage, the team had planted over 100 native keystone species and organised 12 trail cleanups to address erosion and littering. The project also involved partnerships with local businesses, volunteers and nature centres to collect compostable materials.Restoring 15 acres with volunteersAs the project developed, Re:Imagine Inc. expanded its activities from experimentation to hands-on habitat restoration. According to the Barron Prize's 2026 profile, Toake and more than 70 volunteers have worked across 15 acres in northern New Jersey. Their activities have included removing more than two tons of invasive plant biomass, planting over 100 keystone species, repairing erosion damage and maintaining public trails.The restoration work is intended to help native biodiversity recover by reducing the spread of invasive vegetation and creating better conditions for indigenous plants. The volunteers have also helped maintain public green spaces, giving community members opportunities to participate directly in conservation.The project demonstrates how environmental restoration can involve more than developing a scientific solution. Collecting waste, preparing materials, removing invasive plants and maintaining restored areas all require sustained participation from the community.Recognition through the Gloria Barron PrizeToake's work was featured among the runners-up in the 2026 Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes. The award recognises young people across the United States and Canada who have made a positive difference to their communities or the environment. The Barron Prize profile highlighted his efforts to connect scientific research with community service. It also described how Re:Imagine Inc. aims to build a lasting culture of environmental responsibility rather than treating restoration as a one-time activity. Reflecting on the project's development, Toake said his initial effort to restore land had evolved into something more enduring, centred on encouraging people to see themselves as responsible for the environment.Through Re:Imagine Inc., Toake is showing how an idea involving everyday food waste can grow into a wider conservation effort. His initiative brings together scientific experimentation, volunteer participation and habitat restoration, while encouraging other young people to take an active role in protecting local ecosystems.

articles.title: WMO: 2026 set to be one of 4 warmest years on record
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The year 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record, with the past four years, 2023-26, being the top four, the World
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The year 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record, with the past four years, 2023-26, being the top four, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its State of the Climate report released on Monday, the opening day of the 31st session of the UN climate conference (CO) in Antalya, Turkiye.The report showed that each of the past 12 years has been among the warmest on record. It said the global average surface temperature for Jan-Sept 2026 was about 1.47 degrees C above the pre-industrial (1850-1900) average."This figure is likely to rise through the end of the year because of the warming effect of El Nino, which has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December," the WMO said.It underlined that the "protracted streak" of exceptional global temperatures, melting ice and rising sea levels are set to "unleash even more heat and extreme weather" well into 2027.So far, 2024 was the warmest year on record, followed by 2023 and 2025. The report underscored the urgency of taking action to prevent further increase in global average temperatures.The report also highlighted that the global mean sea level had reached a record high in 2026, sea-surface temperatures hit monthly records this year, freshwater storage has been dwindling since 2014 and glaciers lost more than 400 gigatonnes of ice in 2025 - equivalent to approximately 1 mm of sea-level rise. Simply put, this annual mass loss of ice in 2025 would have filled five Olympic-sized pools every second of the year."El Nino and indeed the state of the global climate in 2026 gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts. El Nino doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat from the ocean, which is the warmest ever measured...We are supercharging our weather and El Nino will be a risk multiplier," said WMO secretary-general Celeste Saulo.El Nino is a naturally occurring climatic phenomenon characterised by above-average sea-surface temperatures in central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. It is a major influencer of climate and weather patterns, affecting temperature and rainfall in different regions, and typically has a warming effect on the global climate. In India, it is invariably associated with a weak monsoon and a harsher summer.

articles.title: Fervo now has $12B in orders for its geothermal power tech | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Geothermal company Fervo is targeting natural gas as it brings down geothermal drilling costs at its 8.4 GW resource in Utah.
articles.body:
Geothermal company Fervo couldn’t have picked a better time to deliver its first power plants.

In its third-quarter earnings report, released Monday, the company said it now has $11.9 billion worth of contracted revenue on the books, up from $7.2 billion last quarter.

Fervo has been hitting its deadlines recently, which undoubtedly has helped to drive orders.

As hyperscalers scour the earth for electricity to power their AI data centers, Fervo is on track to complete a 396 megawatt power plant for Google by the end of 2028. The geothermal company connected its first 100 megawatt power plant to the grid earlier this year.

Both projects are built at Cape Station in Utah, a resource that could generate 8.4 gigawatts of electricity. Previously, experts told Fervo the site could only produce about 4 gigawatts .

The Google project, now called Cape Google 400, will be grid connected, co-founder and CEO Tim Latimer said in an earnings call Monday. The arrangement means that Google can draw power from the deal and sell it to other customers if it’s not ready to use it.

“We built Cape Station on our schedule. Google can develop a potential data center on their schedule, and neither party is waiting on the other,” he said.

Latimer’s statement also underlines an advantage that geothermal has over competing generating sources like large nuclear or natural gas power plants — the phased nature of its construction.

Fervo’s newer wells are deeper and hotter, each capable of generating 15 megawatts gross power, and several are linked together into what the company calls a GeoBlock. The first completed GeoBlock generated 33 megawatts, while recent ones hit 50 megawatts. They’re sized to match the demand of a typical data center hall, so hyperscalers can bring them online as they’re completed.

As a business, Fervo is still in the early stages. It ended the quarter with an operating loss of $43.7 million, though it holds cash and cash equivalents of $1.9 billion and long-term debt of $301.6 million, which should give it plenty of runway.

Much will depend on the company bringing down the cost of its power plants. While hyperscalers are hungry for power today, they may not always be as price-indiscriminate.

Yet if Fervo can deliver on its promises, it could end up winning on price. The first phase of its Cape Station project cost $7,000 per kilowatt of capacity, the company said. The cost for its Google project is $5,500 per kilowatt, a significant drop that suggests Fervo is on the right path. With subsidies, that’s about equivalent to a new natural gas power plant running on fuel that costs $6 per million BTUs. Still about twice what natural gas costs today, but trending closer to where it needs to be.

But if Fervo can hit its long-term target of $3,000 per kilowatt, it could significantly undercut natural gas power, even at today’s prices. That’s a pretty ambitious target, but the company has made significant strides in just a few years. No wonder Google is getting in early.

articles.title: The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
articles.summary: At the United Nations climate conference, delegates will consider an international pledge to limit AI’s impact on the environment.﻿
articles.body: At this point, reading through the latest splashy pledge to use AI for the good of the environment feels like downing a nonalcoholic beer. Admittedly, I’m suspicious from the onset. How can this be good? But I love beer and our planet enough to give it a whirl — and hey, why not try a little harm reduction? Negotiators from more than 190 countries around the world are in Antalya, Turkey, this month for the annual United Nations climate summit, called COP31 (the 31st “Conference of the Parties” that ratified the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change). Turkey previewed its Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge ahead of the convening, inviting delegates from other countries to endorse the pledge before its official launch on November 16th. The pledge actually includes some common sense measures that could curb planet-heating pollution from energy-hungry AI data centers. Unfortunately, like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying. At first glance, many of the ingredients you’d expect from a real commitment on AI’s environmental impact are here. It sets out to ensure that data centers are increasingly powered by clean energy, calling for internationally recognized standards for responsible AI development. Similarly, it pushes for reporting requirements so that there’s greater transparency into the impact data centers — which run primarily on fossil fuels — already have on the environment. It even acknowledges the need to manage the tons of e-waste created by the generative AI boom. And yet, there is no there there because, as the text states clearly, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances.” In other words, these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims. There’s also no way this pledge will garner the support of the most influential player in this game (at least for now). The US has way more data centers than any other country, but Donald Trump has pulled the nation out of the global climate accord and has no official delegates at the summit in Turkey. The last point in the pledge is to ensure that advances in generative AI can be used to create more renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in economically developing countries. To that end, research published in a Nature journal in August found that AI causes more carbon emissions by boosting fossil fuel production than it would help avoid through gains in renewable energy. When it comes down to it, this pledge offers a placebo effect at best. In the face of data centers demanding tremendous amounts of electricity and spurring the development of more fossil fuel infrastructure, negotiators can’t be seen as doing nothing about the issue. And with global average temperatures still on the rise, we could all use an emotional support beverage.

articles.title: Anthropic, dona do Claude, tem IPO estimado em US$ 1,4 trilhão, diz agência | G1
articles.standfirst: Oferta pode movimentar até US$ 90,4 bilhões, em meio à desaceleração do entusiasmo dos investidores com empresas de inteligência artificial.
articles.summary: Oferta pode movimentar até US$ 90,4 bilhões, em meio à desaceleração do entusiasmo dos investidores com empresas de inteligência artificial.
articles.body:
A oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO, na sigla em inglês) da Anthropic pode avaliar a empresa em até US$ 1,4 trilhão (R$ 7,8 trilhões), segundo os termos apresentados nesta terça-feira (10).

O valor ficou abaixo das expectativas de alguns investidores , em meio à perda de entusiasmo do mercado com empresas de inteligência artificial (IA).

A companhia, conhecida pelo chatbot Claude , e alguns de seus atuais acionistas pretendem levantar até US$ 64,4 bilhões (R$ 360,6 bilhões) com a venda de 825 milhões de ações. O preço de cada papel deve ficar entre US$ 70 (R$ 392) e US$ 78 (R$ 436,8).

Além disso, a Anthropic pretende captar outros US$ 26 bilhões (R$ 145,6 bilhões) em uma operação separada, por meio da venda de ações a grandes investidores, como Google, Nvidia e AMD.

Somadas as duas operações e os investimentos de acionistas estratégicos, entre eles Broadcom , Micron Technology , Microsoft e TSMC , a oferta poderá movimentar até US$ 90,4 bilhões (R$ 506,2 bilhões).

No limite superior da faixa de preço, a avaliação da empresa chegaria a cerca de US$ 1,4 trilhão , considerando também títulos que podem se transformar em ações, como opções e ações restritas. Sem incluir esses papéis, o valor de mercado seria de aproximadamente US$ 1 trilhão (R$ 5,6 trilhões).

"Ao buscar uma avaliação cerca de 20% abaixo das 'expectativas do mercado', isso permite que os investidores 'elevem os lances' na oferta pública inicial, em vez de enfrentar um cenário do tipo 'pegar ou largar', como aconteceu com a SpaceX", disse Jeff Zell, analista sênior de pesquisa da IPO Boutique.

Anteriormente, investidores chegaram a discutir uma avaliação de até US$ 2 trilhões (R$ 11,2 trilhões) para a Anthropic. As expectativas, porém, diminuíram diante dos altos compromissos financeiros da empresa para construir sua infraestrutura e da recente instabilidade nas ações de companhias ligadas à inteligência artificial.

A abertura de capital também ocorre em um momento de maior dificuldade para empresas que pretendem estrear na bolsa.

Custos mais altos de financiamento, tensões geopolíticas e os rendimentos elevados dos títulos do Tesouro dos Estados Unidos têm pressionado o mercado de IPOs.

Horas antes de a Anthropic apresentar uma versão atualizada de seu prospecto — documento que reúne informações sobre a empresa e os riscos do investimento — à Comissão de Valores Mobiliários dos Estados Unidos (SEC, na sigla em inglês), detalhes da operação circularam brevemente entre bancos de investimento na noite de segunda-feira (9), antes de serem retirados.

As informações constam em e-mails analisados pela Reuters.

Os termos preliminares indicavam que a oferta poderia arrecadar até US$ 69,3 bilhões (R$ 388 bilhões) . O documento atualizado, no entanto, trouxe condições diferentes e uma faixa de preço mais baixa para as ações.

O IPO da Anthropic também é acompanhado de perto por investidores interessados na rival OpenAI. A empresa busca levantar US$ 30 bilhões (R$ 168 bilhões) em sua última rodada de financiamento privado antes de uma possível abertura de capital no início do próximo ano.

No pedido de abertura de capital, a Anthropic adotou o termo "Superinteligência", expressão preferida pelo presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, para se referir à tecnologia .

A escolha ocorre em meio a um cenário político em que a Casa Branca tem apoiado a expansão da inteligência artificial e se oposto a regulamentações para o setor.

O prospecto também detalha riscos para a empresa e para o desenvolvimento da tecnologia. Entre eles, estão a possibilidade de concorrentes avançarem mais rapidamente na criação de modelos de IA e de os progressos da tecnologia superarem a capacidade da Anthropic de implementar medidas adequadas de segurança .

A receita anualizada da empresa era de aproximadamente US$ 81 bilhões (R$ 453,6 bilhões) em 31 de outubro, segundo o documento. O valor representa um aumento de US$ 10 bilhões (R$ 56 bilhões) em relação ao registrado em 30 de setembro.

Apesar do crescimento , a Anthropic tem quase US$ 900 bilhões (R$ 5 trilhões) em compromissos relacionados à capacidade computacional com parceiros como Amazon e Google .

Esses acordos mostram a dimensão da infraestrutura necessária para sustentar a expansão da empresa. Parte dessa capacidade futura depende de financiamentos que não estão sob seu controle.

A decisão de abrir o capital vem na esteira da operação da SpaceX , empresa de Elon Musk , que levantou US$ 75 bilhões (R$ 420 bilhões) e alcançou uma avaliação próxima de US$ 1,75 trilhão (R$ 9,8 trilhões).

A Anthropic foi avaliada em US$ 965 bilhões (R$ 5,4 trilhões) em sua última rodada de financiamento privado. Fundada em 2021, a empresa é comandada pelo presidente-executivo Dario Amodei.

Alguns integrantes do conselho de administração da companhia e entidades ligadas a eles devem comprar até US$ 303 milhões (R$ 1,6 trilhão) em ações.

Goldman Sachs e Morgan Stanley são os principais bancos responsáveis pela operação. Os papéis da Anthropic devem ser negociados na Nasdaq, bolsa de valores dos Estados Unidos, sob o código "ANT".

articles.title: Look to the southeast before sunrise on 15 and 16 November and you can see Mars and Jupiter sitting about 1.2 degrees apart, close enough to spot with the naked eye, no telescope or binoculars are needed
articles.summary: Skywatchers, lose yourself in the sky this November.
articles.body: Skywatchers, lose yourself in the sky this November. Three meteor showers are on the calendar, and on the mornings of 15 and 16 November, Mars and Jupiter will sit just 1.2 degrees apart before dawn, close enough to spot without any equipment, according to NASA’s skywatching guidance for the month. A full supermoon follows on 24 November, the first of three in a row. That’s not all. NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is also approaching an extraordinary milestone.Here’s the November skywatching highlight no true blue sky gazer should miss.Around 12 November: Northern Taurids peak; around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions.15–16 November: Mars and Jupiter appear 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise.17 November: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation.17–18 November: Leonids before dawn after moonset; up to around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions.24 November: Full supermoon; first in a series of three consecutive supermoons.Three meteor showersThis November, you have the chance to spot two more shooting stars: the Northern Taurids and Leonids.The Southern Taurids have already appeared on 5 November. Now the Northern Taurids are expected to follow around 12 November. Both showers typically produce about five meteors per hour under ideal viewing conditions. They are also known for occasional bright fireballs that can light up the night sky.The Leonids, on the other hand, offer the best viewing experience and are expected to peak on 17 and 18 November, in the early hours before dawn and after the Moon has set. Under ideal conditions, you could see up to about 15 meteors per hour, though actual counts are usually lower.If you are particularly interested in seeing them at their best, consider travelling somewhere away from the city lights. Lower levels of light pollution will give you a better view of the meteors. It takes about 30 minutes for your eyes to adjust to the darkness, so keep that in mind when you travel.Mars and JupiterIn a few days, you will also get to see two planets, Mars and Jupiter, side by side. On 15 and 16 November, these planets will appear next to each other in the southeastern sky, creating a spectacle.Mars and Jupiter are separated by enormous distances in space. Their closeness is a matter of alignment. The two planets sit at very different distances from Earth but fall along the same line of sight, so they look like neighbours from our side of the Solar System. The gap, however, is not fixed. Over several consecutive mornings, the pair gradually draws closer before their positions shift and they begin to separate again.The two planets will be separated by about 1.2 degrees in the sky. That gap is slightly wider than the width of two full Moons placed next to each other, which is enough to be seen clearly without optical aid. No telescope or binoculars will be necessary.Jupiter will be the easier of the two to pick out because it is the brighter of the pair. Mars, sitting nearby, has the reddish appearance that makes it recognisable to many observers. Once you find Jupiter, Mars should be easy to locate just beside it.Both planets will be low in the sky, so an unobstructed view of the horizon matters more than height. Dark surroundings help. Streetlights and the glow from buildings wash out faint objects, and Mars is considerably dimmer than Jupiter. Allow your eyes about 30 minutes to adjust before scanning the sky.The planets will be visible in the southeast, so face that direction in the period leading up to sunrise. A clear view of the horizon will help, since both planets will sit low in the sky during these mornings.The supermoon finaleThis November ends with a full supermoon on 24 November. The Moon’s orbit is slightly elliptical, so a full Moon near its closest point can look somewhat larger and brighter. NASA recommends looking towards the eastern horizon around sunset that evening, when the Moon rises. It is the first of three consecutive supermoons, with the next in December and the third in January.Voyager 1 reaches a distance milestoneWell, that’s not all sky gazers should be celebrating this year. NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft reaches a distance of one light-day from Earth on 17 November. This makes it the first human-made object to travel that far. A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours. A radio message from Earth takes a full day to arrive, and a reply needs another day to return, making the round trip roughly 48 hours.NASA is marking the milestone on 17 November with its Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation, which invites the public to celebrate this extraordinary accomplishment in space exploration.

articles.title: Frogs in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest crashed between 1979 and 1982 and no one knew why; nearly 50 years later, scientists tested over 370 preserved museum frogs and found a killer fungus that was absent before 1979
articles.summary: The mystery behind the collapse of various civilisations has troubled scientists to this day.
articles.body: The mystery behind the collapse of various civilisations has troubled scientists to this day. The fall of the Indus Valley Civilisation is still not certain, the most we have are multiple theories around it. Similar is the case with the tale behind evolution, decline and extinction of a few animal species that disappeared in mysterious circumstances within a very short period. The curiosity around these organisms have led the scientists to keep studying their lives even today. The discovery of new species in the current times indicate how nature has a way to stay concealed from humans. One such 50-year-old mystery was unfolded by the scientists about frogs in Brazil’s Atlantic Forest. The population of these frogs declined dramatically between 1979 and 1982 but until now, nobody knew why it happened.The scientists struggled to explain why frogs began disappearing from Brazil’s Atlantic Forest which is actually one of the world’s richest regions for amphibian diversity. The findings published in Molecular Ecology have uncovered evidence that has linked these disappearances to a deadly fungal disease. The study was conducted by researchers at the Center for Conservation Genomics at the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) and Pennsylvania State University (PSU).Who’s behind the decline?Long after the frogs started to decline, a fungus believed to have originated in Asia was formally identified and described in 1999. This microscopic fungus named Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis caused the disease chytridiomycosis, often called chytrid, which is said to be the cause behind the declining frog populations. The pathogen spread in the world during the 1970s and 1980s which led to the beginning of extinction of hundreds of amphibian species around the world. The absence of knowledge about the existence of the pathogen and its late discovery led to difficulty in determining whether it was responsible for these events.Before the discovery of the fungus, some researchers suggested that environmental factors such as climate change or unusually extreme weather might have triggered the declines.Jack Boyette, an NZCBI graduate fellow and doctoral candidate at PSU who led the research told the Science Direct that “While environmental factors could have played a role, our findings most directly implicate the chytrid fungus, revealing that regional invasion of the pathogen coincided with these unexplained amphibian disappearances."The sample for the research were the preserved frogs housed in The Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History. These preserved specimens offered an opportunity to examine the conditions before and after the disappearance events. It helped them track the arrival and spread of the fungus in the forest. More than 370 preserved frogs from 17 species were analysed during the study which aimed to search for spread of chytrid infection and the frequency of its spread.Interesting patternsThe blame was not easily implied to the pathogen when interesting patterns emerged after research. It was revealed that chytrid infection was not observed in specimens collected before 1979. However, in samples from the 1980s more than half tested positive for the fungus. The intriguing fact was that the species which showed the presence of the fungus were the ones whose populations did not decline drastically. Rather, the ones which did not show detectable signs of infection were the ones that suffered the most severe declines.This contradiction is explained by the scientists by concluding that the frogs that were naturally capable of tolerating the infection were able to survive even when the fungus attacked. While others that were more vulnerable could not adapt and hence, few or no infected individuals could ever be collected. Thus, due to the absence of exposure to the fungus and the disease before, chytrid spread rapidly bringing devastating effects for the amphibian species.The latest surveys at Brazil’s Boracéia Biological Station offer a rare glimmer of hope for amphibians. Between 2022 and 2024, researchers from the University of São Paulo revisited the site six times to compare its present-day frog population with historical museum records. Of the 17 species documented in the collection, 12 were found during the new surveys, while the remaining five could not be located. The results suggest that most local amphibian populations have recovered from the devastating declines of the early 1980s, when the chytrid fungus swept through the region. Interestingly, the fungus is still present, but some frog species may have gradually developed greater tolerance to the infection, allowing them to survive despite continued exposure.However, the findings of this discovery are being cautioned to be applied to this particular location. A generalisation of the results is not advisable and cannot automatically explain other disappearances of amphibian populations. Scientists are continuing the investigation into understanding the specifics around the discovery. Researchers are now examining DNA from preserved museum specimens to understand why certain species were more vulnerable while others managed to survive.

articles.title: Sariska lost all its tigers to poaching by 2005 and had to bring them back from Ranthambore in 2008; now tigress ST-26 has been filmed with her first two cubs, taking the reserve’s tiger count to 58
articles.summary: While hunting was a prestigious sport for the royals of the older times, their enjoyment cost the ecosystem and its inhabitants in irreversible ways.
articles.body: While hunting was a prestigious sport for the royals of the older times, their enjoyment cost the ecosystem and its inhabitants in irreversible ways. However, fortunately, the modern world became more conscious about nature and started looking at preserving the balance in natural habitats. This consciousness has provided us with incredible conservation stories, especially in India where landscapes are full of varied wildlife, from sensitive Himalayan species to an abundance in the Western Ghats. One such conservation success story comes from regal Rajasthan for the conservation of India's national pride, the Tiger.Welcome to Sariska Tiger Reserve, located roughly 200 km from Delhi, it is a wildlife escape in Rajasthan’s Alwar district. The tiger reserve became the site for the World’s First Tiger Relocation program in 2008 and is today studied as a successful case study. The strategy's success was declared in 2012 itself when tigress ST2 gave birth to 2 cubs. Now, the tiger population has reached 58 with ST-26 being filmed with her two newborn cubs last month. The moment feels like completing a full cycle as the 6-7 year old tigress was herself born in Sariska.The sanctuary of wildlifeSariska used to serve as the hunting ground for the princely state of Alwar. The very first mention of the region goes way back to the Prahlad-Hiranyakashap story, and the Pandavas’ year-long exile in secrecy in Mahabharat (Virat Nagar). The region eventually gained prominence when it came under the control of the Bargujar Kings, who were part of the huge Gujara Pratihara empire in northern India.After independence, conservation efforts began with it being notified as a Wildlife Reserve in 1955. Its status was raised in 1958 with recognition as a Wildlife Sanctuary. Finally, it came under Project Tiger in 1979 and became Sariska Tiger Reserve. The landscape at the reserve is unlike other forests, it is dry the majority of the year. During summer, temperatures can even reach 45°C as the jungle turns ash brown due to heat. However , the monsoon season brings some relief to the region.The tiger comeback storyBy 2005, tigers had disappeared from the reserve. Their local extinction was a devastating setback, raising difficult questions about wildlife protection and the future of the landscape. Yet the story did not end there.In 2008, a pioneering programme began reintroducing tigers from Ranthambore to Sariska. The effort involved scientific planning, monitoring and continued protection, marking an important experiment in restoring a species to a landscape where it had vanished. According to a June 2026 announcement by India’s Press Information Bureau, Sariska had recovered to support 56 tigers, 18 years after the reintroduction programme began. The initiative is recognised as a landmark in wildlife conservation and a source of lessons for future tiger-recovery efforts. This number increased to 58 with two new cubs observed last month.This turned out to be the world’s first successful tiger relocation project, made possible by intricate planning, habitat protection, wildlife monitoring and local community efforts. A visit to Sariska becomes more meaningful when you see it not merely as a place to photograph a tiger, but as a landscape still working to protect its wildlife.Planning your Sariska adventureThe best way to explore the reserve is on an authorised jeep or canter safari. Winter, broadly from October to March, is a comfortable period for exploring the region, although mornings can be chilly. Summer can be hot, but wildlife activity around water sources may make it appealing to some visitors. Safari availability and timings vary by season, and visitors should check current rules before travelling.How to reach: Sariska lies in Alwar district, Rajasthan.By Air: Jaipur International Airport is the nearest airport to Sariska. It is located approximately 133 km away from the reserve. After you land, you can hire a taxi or catch a bus to reach the reserve.By Train: Alwar Junction is the nearest railway station and around 35 km from Sariska. Enough trains are available from major cities, including Delhi, Jaipur and Mumbai. From the station, taxis and local buses will be available to take you to Sariska.By Road: Sariska enjoys good road connectivity with several cities and towns across Rajasthan and neighbouring states.If travelling from Delhi, take NH48 (Delhi-Jaipur Highway) and continue via the Alwar-Bhiwadi Bypass Road. From Jaipur, follow NH48 and then take the Alwar-Jaipur Road towards the reserve.

articles.title: Scientists rescued about 160 tadpoles from the ashes of Australia's Black Summer fires, raised the rare species in captivity and have now released 53 giant burrowing frogs into the forests where they were found
articles.summary: Scientists rescued about 160 tadpoles from the ashes of Australia's Black Summer fires, raised the rare species in captivity and have now released 53
articles.body: Scientists rescued about 160 tadpoles from the ashes of Australia's Black Summer fires, raised the rare species in captivity and have now released 53 giant burrowing frogs into the forests where they were foundThe aftermath of a devastating wildfire can leave more than scorched trees and damaged landscapes. Sometimes, it reveals unexpected survivors. In Australia's East Gippsland region, a discovery made among the remains of the catastrophic 2019–2020 Black Summer bushfires has grown into an extraordinary conservation success. Nearly six years after the fires devastated their habitat, 53 critically endangered Southern Giant Burrowing Frogs have returned to the forests, following years of specialist care and a pioneering captive-breeding programme.From fire survivors to conservation successAccording to ABC News, the frogs were originally discovered as approximately 160 tadpoles in small pockets of water after the fires destroyed extensive areas of their natural habitat. Despite the widespread destruction, the surviving tadpoles offered scientists an opportunity to protect a species whose numbers were already under pressure.Herpetologist Matt Clancy of Snowline Ecology took the rescued tadpoles to Healesville Sanctuary in 2021. According to reports, Zoos Victoria's Melbourne Zoo and Healesville Sanctuary amphibian goalkeepers adapted to captivity.The first Southern Giant Burrowing Frog captive breeding occurred in 2025, marking another program milestone. Zoos Victoria described the achievement as a world first, marking an important step towards securing the species' future.An elusive species facing multiple threatsDespite its name, the Southern Giant Burrowing Frog is a relatively compact amphibian, with adults roughly the size of a cricket ball and has large eyes, muscular limbs, and a bright yellow body.According to Zoos Victoria, the species is native to south-eastern Australia, with its range extending from areas south of Kangaroo Valley in New South Wales through Victoria to Walhalla in central Gippsland.However, estimating its remaining population is particularly challenging. As ABC News reported, these frogs spend much of their lives underground, emerging primarily to breed following heavy rainfall. Males can sometimes be detected calling for just one night before disappearing underground for years.Habitat destruction, prolonged drought, bushfires and chytridiomycosis, a widespread amphibian disease, have all contributed to declining populations. Victoria currently has fewer than five known breeding sites.Returning home with a scientific purposeThe release of 53 frogs is not simply a return to their original habitat. It also gives researchers an opportunity to understand more about their movements, survival and breeding behaviour.Zoos Victoria explained that each released frog received a microchip or passive integrated transponder (PIT) tag. These identifiers will allow researchers to recognise individual animals during future population surveys and establish how far they have travelled from their release locations.Song meters have also been installed throughout the forest to record the frogs' distinctive calls and help field teams locate potential breeding sites.The conservation partnership between Zoos Victoria and Snowline Ecology has therefore moved into a crucial new phase. With the frogs now sexually mature and their genetics secured for future generations, researchers hope they will contribute to rebuilding wild populations, the ABC News report states. Also, it is reported that the Wildlife and Habitat Bushfire Recovery Program of Australia funded the project.Images Courtesy: Zoos Victoria
