articles.title: India’s Aditya-L1 unlocks Sun's secrets: How new discovery could help predict solar storms that threaten Earth
articles.summary: The Sun may be millions of kilometres away, but powerful eruptions on its surface can have consequences for life on Earth.
articles.body: The Sun may be millions of kilometres away, but powerful eruptions on its surface can have consequences for life on Earth. From satellite-based navigation and communication to electricity networks, several technologies people depend on can be affected when these eruptions send enormous amounts of charged particles towards our planet.India's Aditya-L1 solar mission has helped scientists uncover a previously hidden aspect of how these eruptions behave. The discovery could help researchers better understand how solar storms travel through space and, eventually, improve predictions of when they might reach Earth.Scientists from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru, found that a solar eruption observed in August 2024 did not expand uniformly like a symmetrical bubble. Instead, it expanded unevenly, developing an asymmetric shape.The finding, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, challenges a commonly used assumption about how these eruptions expand close to the Sun. Researchers arrived at the conclusion by combining observations from Aditya-L1's Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC), images from Nasa's Solar Dynamics Observatory and three-dimensional modelling.But why does the shape of an eruption matter? And how could understanding its movement help scientists predict solar storms that can disrupt satellites, navigation systems and power infrastructure?What are solar eruptions and why do they matter?The Sun is not a completely stable ball of hot gas. Its magnetic field is constantly changing, creating conditions that can trigger powerful eruptions from its outer atmosphere.One such phenomenon is a coronal mass ejection (CME). It involves the release of enormous quantities of hot, magnetised plasma from the Sun's outermost atmospheric layer, known as the corona. These eruptions can travel through interplanetary space at high speeds, carrying magnetic fields and charged particles with them.When a CME is directed towards Earth, it can interact with the planet's magnetic field and trigger a geomagnetic storm. The strength of the disturbance depends on several factors, including the speed and magnetic properties of the incoming eruption.Such storms are not merely astronomical events. They can affect technologies that modern societies increasingly depend on, particularly those operating in space or relying on satellite-based systems.Satellites can experience disruptions to their operations and, in severe cases, damage to onboard electronics. Solar activity can also affect radio communications and interfere with the accuracy of satellite-based navigation systems such as GPS. Strong geomagnetic disturbances can induce electrical currents in power transmission networks, potentially putting transformers and other grid equipment under stress.The effects can extend to aviation, particularly high-frequency radio communications and operations on polar routes, where exposure to space-weather disturbances can be greater.Chethan Kumar, a space expert and journalist who has extensively covered the extraterrestrial field, said solar storms can affect several systems simultaneously, including electricity supplies, radio signals and satellite-based applications.“Solar storms are also known to interfere with positioning services, so your GPS can get affected. When GPS gets affected, your air travel becomes less reliable, and it's a cascading effect,” he said.This makes the ability to monitor and forecast solar activity important for satellite operators, communication networks, aviation authorities and power-grid managers.However, predicting the behaviour of a CME after it leaves the Sun remains a complex scientific challenge. Scientists need to establish not only where an eruption is heading but also how fast it is moving and how its structure changes as it travels through space.Why are solar storms difficult to predict?One of the biggest challenges in studying CMEs is understanding their movement in three dimensions, particularly during the initial stages of an eruption.Scientists use instruments called coronagraphs to observe CMEs. These instruments block the bright solar disc, allowing researchers to study the much fainter corona and track eruptions as they move away from the Sun.However, conventional coronagraph images primarily capture movement across the observer's field of view. In other words, they show how an eruption travels across the sky but cannot directly establish how fast the plasma is moving towards or away from the observer.This missing information is important because a CME is a three-dimensional structure, not a flat object moving across an image.Two eruptions that appear similar in conventional images could have different three-dimensional shapes and expansion patterns. Their interactions with the surrounding solar wind could therefore differ, potentially affecting how their speeds change during propagation.Scientists have traditionally relied on observations from multiple spacecraft positioned at different locations to reconstruct the three-dimensional evolution of CMEs. While this provides valuable information, studying eruptions close to the Sun remains particularly challenging because they evolve rapidly during these early stages.This is where Aditya-L1's VELC instrument offers an additional observational capability.How Aditya-L1 uncovered the hidden dimensionVELC is one of the primary scientific instruments onboard Aditya-L1. It was developed by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics in Bengaluru, with substantial support from Isro.Unlike instruments that only capture images, VELC also records spectra, allowing scientists to study changes in the wavelength of light emitted by the solar corona.The technique is known as Doppler spectroscopy. It is based on the principle that the wavelength of light changes depending on the movement of the source relative to the observer.For instance, when plasma moves towards an observer, the light it emits shifts towards shorter wavelengths, known as a blue shift. When it moves away, the wavelength shifts towards the longer, red end of the spectrum.This allows scientists to measure movement along the line of sight, the direction between the observed object and the observer, which conventional images cannot directly reveal.During the CME observed on August 5, 2024, VELC detected an unusual pattern in the spectrum. Researchers observed two distinct branches of emission appearing simultaneously on opposite sides of the regular coronal emission line.One branch was shifted towards shorter wavelengths, indicating plasma moving towards the observer, while the other shifted towards longer wavelengths, indicating plasma moving away.The observations suggested that different parts of the expanding CME were moving in opposite directions along the line of sight.Meanwhile, images captured by Nasa's Solar Dynamics Observatory showed how the eruption was propagating across the sky.The researchers combined the two sets of observations to understand the eruption's three-dimensional behaviour.To interpret the unusual spectral pattern, the IIA team developed a three-dimensional geometric and kinematic model of the expanding shell-like CME structure. They varied the model's parameters to determine which configuration could reproduce the observations recorded by VELC.The results showed that a symmetrical expansion could not adequately explain the observed spectral features. However, when the researchers introduced a tilted structure and asymmetric lateral expansion, the simulated spectra closely matched the actual observations.The combination of spectroscopic measurements, solar images and three-dimensional modelling provided evidence that the CME had expanded non-uniformly in the low corona, the region of the Sun's outer atmosphere closest to its visible surface.Why does the shape of a solar eruption matter?The discovery is important because the shape and expansion of a CME can influence how it travels through the heliosphere, the vast region of space dominated by the Sun's solar wind and magnetic field.As a CME moves away from the Sun, it interacts with the surrounding solar wind. These interactions can affect its speed, with the solar wind exerting a drag force on the expanding structure.An eruption's shape and expansion pattern could influence the extent of this interaction. A CME expanding differently in different directions may therefore experience different levels of drag compared with one expanding uniformly.This can make it more difficult to estimate how its speed will change during its journey towards Earth.For scientists monitoring space weather, even small differences in the estimated speed and trajectory of a CME can matter when calculating its potential arrival time.Understanding the eruption's three-dimensional structure close to the Sun could therefore help improve models used to track its subsequent movement through space.The latest study does not establish that all CMEs expand asymmetrically. It examines one particular eruption observed on August 5, 2024. However, it provides evidence that assuming a symmetrical, bubble-like expansion may not always accurately represent how these structures evolve.Further observations will be needed to establish how frequently such asymmetric expansion occurs and how significantly it affects CME propagation.Can satellites protect themselves from solar storms?Satellite operators make preparations to deal with space-weather events, but these measures have limitations, particularly during very large solar storms.Kumar said satellites are equipped with thermal protection and operators use space-weather predictions to plan for potential disturbances. When forecasts indicate a threat, operators may attempt to change a satellite's orbit or direction.“But if there's a massive event, no matter what you do, your planning doesn't work,” he said.He added that orbit manoeuvres, including moving satellites to a higher orbit or changing their direction, can be expensive and may not always work.Referring to the impact of solar storms on Starlink satellites, Kumar said there are instances when replacing disrupted satellites can be a more practical option for operators able to launch new ones frequently.He said the effects of solar storms should not be presented as an inevitable catastrophe for space infrastructure.Kumar added that solar storms have existed for as long as the Sun and that satellites have been operating for around 70 years. Such events can pose a threat, but that does not mean every satellite will be affected or destroyed when a large CME occurs.Could Aditya-L1 help improve solar-storm forecasts?The broader significance of the research lies in its potential contribution to space-weather forecasting.Scientists need to understand the direction, speed and expansion of a CME to estimate whether it could reach Earth and when it might arrive. Better observations of its early evolution could help refine the models used to make these predictions.If researchers can reliably reconstruct the three-dimensional geometry of CMEs using VELC's spectroscopic measurements, it could provide an additional way to study eruptions without depending entirely on observations from multiple spacecraft positioned at different vantage points.This information could eventually be useful for agencies monitoring space weather and organisations responsible for operating satellites, communication networks and power infrastructure.For India, which increasingly relies on satellite-based services for navigation, telecommunications, weather monitoring and disaster management, improving the understanding of solar activity has wider technological significance.However, the research is an early step towards that goal rather than a ready-to-use solar-storm warning system. The study has demonstrated how VELC can help constrain the three-dimensional geometry of an eruption by combining spectroscopy with imaging observations. It has not yet been established that the instrument can independently predict the precise arrival time or potential impact of an Earth-directed CME.Isro said further studies would help establish how reliably VELC spectroscopy can determine the propagation direction, velocity and expansion of CMEs.By providing a new way to examine how solar eruptions evolve close to the Sun, Aditya-L1 could help scientists build a more complete picture of these powerful events. The eventual goal is to understand their behaviour well enough to improve predictions of their journey through space, and prepare better for the disturbances they could cause when they reach Earth.

articles.title: Einstein's Equations Reveal Gravity Can Break And Reconnect Like Magnetic Fields
articles.summary: Relativity still has some tricks up its sleeve.
articles.body:
Everywhere you go in the Universe, gravity exists.

It's inextricably woven into its fabric, forming stars and planets, and choreographing the dance of galaxies.

It's what keeps our world together and us upon it – yet even after more than a century of studying gravity by way of Einstein's theory of general relativity, scientists are still discovering surprising new ways it can behave.

But a new discovery by physicists Luca Comisso of Columbia University and Felipe A. Asenjo of Adolfo Ibáñez University in Chile may take the relativity biscuit.

Their new calculations suggest that gravitational fields may be able to break and reconnect in new configurations – just like magnetic fields do on the Sun.

"We are not modifying general relativity or introducing new physics beyond it. Rather, we are identifying physical principles that have remained unrecognized for more than a century," Comisso told ScienceAlert.

Our everyday experience of gravity is of a force that keeps us more or less on the ground. But there's more to it than just attraction. According to relativity, gravity is described by a field – the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy, which influences how matter and light move through the Universe.

The equations describing this curvature are a masterpiece of physics, allowing physicists to predict everything from the bending of starlight to the gravitational waves produced by colliding black holes – and they've survived test after test in the classical Universe.

But the Universe has other kinds of fields, too.

We only have to look to the Sun to find some – vast magnetic fields threading through the charged solar plasma, whose tangled strands can break and reconnect in a process called magnetic reconnection, unleashing the energy that powers solar flares.

And, as Comisso and Asenjo have now demonstrated mathematically, gravity may have a similar trick in its repertoire.

"We had suspected that gravity might share some properties with magnetic fields, since it has long been known that Einstein's equations can be rewritten in forms that resemble the equations of electromagnetism," Comisso explained.

"However, we did not know how far this analogy would extend. It was only after working through the analytical calculations, step by step at the blackboard, that we realized just how closely gravitational fields could follow the same principles that govern magnetic fields in plasmas."

The revelation began with an earlier paper the pair published alongside a third co-author, physicist Maricarmen A. Winkler of Adolfo Ibáñez University.

Their calculations showed that, under certain conditions, gravitational fields can behave as though their connections are frozen in place, preserving the links between different regions even as spacetime evolves.

They realized that this behavior has a striking analog in the magnetic fields of electrically charged plasma, where field lines can remain connected even as the plasma flows and changes shape.

But, as we have already established, magnetic fields don't always behave this way. When the conditions that keep their field lines connected break down, those connections can rearrange themselves through magnetic reconnection, changing which regions are linked by the magnetic field.

So, it seemed natural to wonder if the same could be true of gravity, too.

To find out, Comisso and Asenjo returned to Einstein's equations, using a mathematical formulation that reveals similarities between gravity and electromagnetism.

They investigated what happens when the conditions that preserve gravitational field connections break down, and found that, under certain circumstances, the fields can reconnect in new configurations – a process they call gravitational reconnection.

"Instead of lines extending through three-dimensional space, the gravitational field forms sheets extending through four-dimensional spacetime (three dimensions of space and one of time)," Comisso explained.

"Like magnetic field lines, these sheets are not physical objects, but mathematical structures that help us visualize the gravitational field. As spacetime evolves, these sheets can stretch, bend, and, under certain conditions, break and reconnect in a new arrangement."

"This does not mean that spacetime itself tears apart, but rather that the gravitational field changes how different regions of spacetime are connected."

If this process occurs in the Universe, its effects wouldn't necessarily be something we could see or even feel. Even the gravitational ripples from colliding black holes – arguably the most hefty events the Universe can pull off – change the length of LIGO's 4-kilometer arms by less than the width of a proton.

But the physics implications, now – there, we're talking.

Physicists can currently use supercomputers to simulate the dramatic changes in spacetime that accompany massive events like black hole collisions or core-collapse supernovae.

But being able to calculate how spacetime evolves doesn't necessarily reveal the underlying physical mechanisms responsible for energy transfer.

This is where gravitational reconnection could be useful, and magnetic reconnection on the Sun gives a real-world example. Physicists can simulate the behavior of solar plasma, but identifying magnetic reconnection as a mechanism responsible for releasing its energy gives them a deeper understanding of what is happening and why.

"What I find particularly remarkable is that these principles give us a new way to understand the complex dynamics of spacetime in relatively simple physical terms," Comisso said.

"Just as magnetic reconnection has transformed our understanding of how magnetic energy is released in plasmas, gravitational reconnection could provide a similarly powerful framework for understanding how gravitational fields evolve and exchange energy and momentum with matter."

There's still a great deal to learn, however. For now, gravitational reconnection is a theoretical possibility, not a phenomenon that scientists have observed in nature.

The researchers believe gravitational reconnection could occur in a variety of astrophysical settings, such as merging black holes or collapsing stars.

Numerical simulations, Comisso said, could help identify the conditions under which it happens and characterize how the process unfolds.

One particularly tantalizing possibility is that gravitational reconnection might leave a distinctive signature in the gravitational waves emitted by colliding black holes. If it does, those simulations might reveal what to look for in LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA data.

"Our work provides the theoretical foundations for gravitational reconnection, but we still need to determine the precise conditions under which it occurs in nature and understand its role in astrophysical phenomena," Comisso said.

"For us, this is one of the most exciting questions that our research has opened up, and one we are eager to investigate further."

The research has been published in Physical Review D .

articles.title: A rare Jamaican iguana was once thought extinct and fewer than 50 survived when it was rediscovered in 1990; after decades of captive rearing and predator control, its 1,000th release is planned for Saturday
articles.summary: A reptile that was once declared extinct is finally approaching a conservation milestone in Jamaica.
articles.body: A reptile that was once declared extinct is finally approaching a conservation milestone in Jamaica. The country's critically endangered Jamaican rock iguana, which was rediscovered in 1990 after fewer than 50 individuals were found in the wild, is set to reach its 1,000th head-started release on November 14. The National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA), which coordinates the recovery programme with local and international partners, will return the iguanas to their natural habitat in the Hellshire Hills, St Catherine, after decades of captive rearing, habitat protection and predator control.According to the Jamaica Observer, 973 head-started iguanas have already been released into the wild, with another 114 scheduled for Saturday's exercise. The milestone marks more than three decades of conservation work for a species that had disappeared from much of its former range. Jamaica's Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change, Matthew Samuda, described the upcoming release as the result of years of scientific research, habitat management and collaboration.From presumed extinction to rediscoveryThe Jamaican rock iguana, scientifically known as Cyclura collei, is endemic to Jamaica, meaning it is found naturally nowhere else in the world. It is also the island's largest native animal, growing up to around five feet in length. Its body is generally dark-coloured, with a long tail and distinctive rows of spines running along its back.The species was declared extinct in 1948 after its population collapsed. The decline had been driven largely by introduced predators and habitat destruction. Mongooses, cats and stray dogs prey on iguana eggs and young hatchlings, while pigs can also threaten nests. The clearing of forests for agriculture, housing and charcoal production further reduced the habitat available to the reptiles.However, in 1990, researchers rediscovered a surviving population in the remote Hellshire Hills of southern Jamaica. Fewer than 50 individuals, most of them older adults, were found, raising concerns that the reptile could disappear permanently without urgent intervention. The Hellshire Hills, which contain the Caribbean's largest dry forest, became the centre of the recovery effort. The area provides the vegetation and nesting grounds the iguanas need, but protecting the remaining wild population required more than simply preventing further habitat loss.How captive rearing gives hatchlings a second chanceA central part of Jamaica's recovery strategy is a conservation technique known as 'head-starting'. Under this programme, hatchlings are collected from the wild and raised in a protected environment at the Headstart Facility at Hope Zoo in Kingston. They are cared for until they grow large and strong enough to have a better chance of surviving when returned to their natural habitat. Young iguanas are particularly vulnerable to predators, making the early stages of their lives a critical period. Raising them away from mongooses, cats and other invasive animals allows more individuals to reach a size at which they are less likely to be killed after release.The programme, which began releasing head-started iguanas in 1996, is coordinated by NEPA and supported by organisations including Hope Zoo, Fort Worth Zoo, the International Iguana Foundation and other conservation partners. Fort Worth Zoo has been involved in the effort since 1993, providing scientific expertise and support for the recovery programme. The facility currently cares for approximately 250 to 300 juvenile iguanas, according to the Jamaica Observer. Each animal is part of a carefully managed process that involves raising, monitoring and eventually returning it to the wild.Removing predators and protecting nestsCaptive rearing alone cannot ensure the species' survival if the threats in its natural habitat remain. Conservation teams have therefore combined the head-start programme with predator control and protection of nesting sites.In the Hellshire Hills, NEPA and its partners monitor more than 280 live predator traps. The Jamaica Observer reported that more than 1,500 invasive predators have been removed from the iguanas' core habitat over time. The effort focuses particularly on Indian mongooses and feral cats, which can kill hatchlings and destroy eggs.Conservationists also monitor nesting sites and maintain suitable artificial nesting areas to improve the chances of successful reproduction. The programme tracks released animals to understand how well they adapt to the wild and whether the population is reproducing independently.Iguana conservation specialist Tandora Del Grant, who has been involved in the project since 1995, told the Jamaica Observer that the survival and reproduction of released animals in the wild were encouraging signs. However, she stressed that continued conservation work would be necessary to prevent the population from declining again.The Jamaican rock iguana is important not only as a rare native species but also because of its role in maintaining the ecosystem. It feeds largely on fruits, leaves and other plant material, helping disperse seeds through its droppings. This supports the regeneration of trees and vegetation across the dry forest.NEPA ranger Jomo Pinkney highlighted this role in comments reported by the Jamaica Observer, explaining that iguanas help spread seeds after eating fruit. Their presence therefore contributes to the health and regeneration of the very habitat on which they depend.Despite the progress, the species remains classified as critically endangered. Its natural range is extremely restricted, and invasive predators, habitat degradation and human activity continue to pose threats. The International Iguana Foundation identifies the Hellshire Hills as the species' remaining stronghold.Conservationists are now looking towards another potential milestone: reintroducing the iguanas to Goat Island, which could provide an additional safe habitat and sanctuary for the population. A move like this would require careful preparation, particularly ensuring that invasive predators are removed before iguanas are introduced.

articles.title: Heavy rainfall could speed up an Alaskan glacier by 215%, with surges lasting up to 66 hours; scientists explain how rainfall accelerates ice flow
articles.summary: Heavy rainfall can push a glacier in Alaska to more than double its speed for a short time, according to new research.
articles.body: Heavy rainfall can push a glacier in Alaska to more than double its speed for a short time, according to new research. Rainfall can accelerate the glacier's movement by as much as 251%, the study found. Scientists from Boise State University studied Sít’ Kusá, also known as Turner Glacier, and found that rainfall often triggers sudden surges in its movement. The research is published in the journal The Cryosphere.Glacier movementsMost people think of glaciers as slow, heavy masses of ice that shape valleys over thousands of years. While that is usually true, occasionally, a glacier surges and moves many times faster than normal. Such surges can cause significant damage. They can gouge out valleys, split the surface into deep cracks and block side valleys. The blocked water can form temporary lakes, and when those ice dams break, the result can be flooding.Understanding the mechanisms behind these surges is therefore vital for scientists monitoring instabilities in glaciers around the world and their wider implications for climate change.Parker Wilkerson of Boise State University and his colleagues decided to investigate this phenomenon. They placed GPS instruments around the glacier. The devices recorded its position every 15 seconds, helping the researchers track rapid changes in speed and compare them with the glacier's slower, long-term pace.The team then matched those speed changes with rainfall. They checked their rainfall estimates against readings from the weather station at nearby Yakutat Airport. The results were clear: more than half of the rainfall events they studied led to an increase in speed.A surge that lasted longerThe researchers compared a surge period from 2020 to 2021 with a slower period from 2022 to 2024. During the surge, the glacier's peak daily speed reached 7.5 metres (24.6 feet). That represented a 116% increase in a single day, or more than double its normal speed.The researchers also found that the surge lasted 66 hours, about twice as long as any surge during the slower period. They observed that it usually began about 12 hours after rainfall started, once at least 20 millimetres (0.79 inches) had fallen. The glacier returned to a stable state three days later.Even during the quieter period, rainfall sometimes accelerated the ice. These speed-ups required more rainfall, at least 60 millimetres (2.4 inches) from the start of the event. They also peaked later, about 32 hours after the rain began, on average. The increase was smaller in real terms, at 1.5 metres per day. Yet the percentage increase was 251%. This is because the glacier normally moves so slowly that even a modest push makes a large difference in percentage terms.The researchers also found that the steepest, lowest parts of the glacier accelerated the most. They suggested that this was due to a combination of the land's shape, gravity and meltwater helping the ice move.What dynamic drainage doesThe study found that drainage is a pivotal factor. When a glacier's drainage system works well, channels run across, through and beneath the ice, carrying rainwater and meltwater away quickly. The ice stays in contact with the bedrock and maintains a steady pace.When drainage is poor, water becomes trapped in pockets beneath the ice or in the sediment below, known as till. Pressure builds as more water arrives, pushing against the weight of the ice. This reduces friction, allowing the ice to slide over the ground.The researchers now want to investigate these links further because changing weather patterns could make such surges more common. More rainfall, combined with increased melting in a warmer world, could mean greater ice loss and rising sea levels over time. Coastal and island communities would feel the effects first.“We find that particularly large and prolonged rain events can cause temporary slow-downs during the surge, but that speeds return to pre-event levels in less than two weeks as the drainage system reverts to its inefficient state. Our work supports recent analyses of glacier instabilities suggesting there isn't a binary switch in drainage system configuration during surges. More broadly, our findings expand our understanding of glacier kinematic responses to rainfall, demonstrating that rain events can modulate speeds of both fast- and slow-flowing glaciers,” they concluded.

articles.title: Starlink Mini 2 adds a swappable battery
articles.summary: The new Starlink Mini 2 dish adds a built-in rechargeable battery so you can connect to satellite internet for over four hours.
articles.body: SpaceX announced a new version of its all-in-one satellite internet terminal that integrates a dish, Wi-Fi router, and now a battery into a single device about the size of a laptop. According to some users on X who shared screenshots of invitations to order Starlink Mini 2, the dish is priced at $999, which includes a full year of Roam Unlimited service that SpaceX values at $2,100. The Starlink Mini 2 will run for up to 4.5 hours on a full charge, SpaceX claims, but that can be expanded by hot-swapping in additional batteries that will be sold separately, or by connecting the dish to a 60W power source over USB-C. Despite the addition of an integrated battery, the Starlink Mini 2 dish is thinner than the original Mini. SpaceX has managed to slim it down to 23.1mm thick, while the previous version of the Mini was 38.5mm. The Starlink Mini 2 is slightly heavier at around 3.5 pounds as a result of the added battery weight, but carries forward an IP67 dust- and waterproof rating so it’s still safe to use outdoors. Preorders are now open “by invitation for select US customers,” according to the Starlink website, but “coming soon” to more customers and countries.

articles.title: A 3,000-year-old Spanish treasure contains two unusual iron objects; chemical tests suggest they may have been crafted from metal that fell to Earth in meteorites
articles.summary: Two iron objects found in a Spanish treasure discovered in 1963 may have been made from metal that arrived on Earth from space.
articles.body: Two iron objects found in a Spanish treasure discovered in 1963 may have been made from metal that arrived on Earth from space. The objects, a hollow hemisphere and an open bracelet, form part of the Villena Treasure, a major collection of Bronze Age goldwork found in Alicante, in southeastern Spain. Their iron-like appearance had raised questions about the treasure’s age, as terrestrial iron production began later than the period in which the collection may have been buried.The findings were published in a research paper in Trabajos de Prehistoria, titled ‘Meteoritic iron in the Villena Treasure?’, which examined the chemical composition of both objects. The results are compatible with a Late Bronze Age date, before widespread terrestrial iron production began.What makes two iron objects in Spain's Bronze Age treasure unusualThe Villena Treasure was discovered by José M.ª Soler at Rambla del Panadero in late 1963 and is held at the Villena Museum in Alicante. It is one of the most important collections of Bronze Age goldwork in the Iberian Peninsula. The two objects are a hollow hemisphere covered with a pierced gold sheet and an open bracelet.The hemisphere has been interpreted as the top of a sceptre or staff of authority, or as a sword hilt. The bracelet has a flat-convex cross-section and rounded, slightly flattened ends. Both objects have iron-like surfaces affected by corrosion. Their presence created a dating problem because researchers had to establish whether the material was terrestrial or meteoritic iron used to make them.How did scientists test the Spanish treasure's iron objects for meteoritic metalMeteoritic iron occurs in certain meteorites and is mainly an iron-nickel alloy. Its nickel content is usually above 5% by weight, and it also contains smaller amounts of other elements, including cobalt. Terrestrial iron generally has low or undetectable nickel levels. Researchers collected tiny samples of corrosion from both Villena objects in 2007, with the museum's permission. Initial portable X-ray fluorescence tests detected iron and nickel, but the samples were too small for reliable measurements.The researchers later sent them to a specialist laboratory in Mannheim, Germany, for laser ablation inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. This method can detect very small quantities of elements and trace elements needed to classify meteorites. Both samples weighed only fractions of a milligram each.Nickel measurements provide clues to the meteoritic origins of the two iron objectsThe first laboratory results suggested that the hollow hemisphere contained 5.5% nickel, leading the specialist who examined the data to consider it possibly meteoritic. The bracelet contained 2.8% nickel, which was initially considered too little for meteoritic iron. Researchers therefore obtained permission to take a second sample from the bracelet in 2013, going deeper into its corrosion layer.An X-ray fluorescence analysis of this sample produced a higher nickel result. The researchers noted that nickel levels can increase towards the interior of corroded meteoritic iron. They then compared the objects' nickel-to-iron and nickel-to-cobalt ratios with data for meteorites and prehistoric iron objects. Both objects fell within the meteoritic iron distribution region. The researchers also examined gallium, germanium and ruthenium levels.Chemical findings support the possible Bronze Age origins of the two iron artefactsThe analyses indicate, with a high degree of probability, that both objects were made from meteoritic iron. Similar levels of minor and trace elements, particularly gallium, germanium and ruthenium, may point to a common origin. The researchers said the findings are compatible with a Late Bronze Age date, before widespread production of terrestrial iron began.They linked this dating possibility to the relationship between the Villena Treasure and the Cabezo Redondo Treasure, whose settlement was abandoned before 1200 cal BC. However, they said further tests would be needed to increase certainty. These could include non-invasive techniques such as gamma spectrometry, proton-induced X-ray emission, computed tomography, and muon radiography.

articles.title: In 2006, a developer planned more than 200 homes on a 229-acre South Carolina tract bordering a wildlife refuge; after 20 years of opposition, it has agreed to sell the land for permanent conservation
articles.summary: A 229-acre stretch of land in South Carolina that was once intended for a large residential development is now set to be preserved for wildlife and future
articles.body: A 229-acre stretch of land in South Carolina that was once intended for a large residential development is now set to be preserved for wildlife and future generations. The property, known as the White Tract, sits next to the Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge in Awendaw, Charleston County. A proposal to build approximately 208 single-family homes on part of the property triggered years of opposition from conservation groups concerned about the impact of construction on the surrounding wetlands, wildlife and water quality.The South Carolina Environmental Law Project (SCELP), which represented conservation organisations in legal challenges against the development, announced the agreement on November 6, 2026, in a joint press release with the Coastal Conservation League, Charleston Waterkeeper and Friends of Coastal South Carolina. Under the settlement, developer Pulte Home Company has agreed to sell the White Tract to the nonprofit Open Space Institute for permanent conservation. The agreement brings a long-running dispute closer to an end, although the transaction has yet to be completed.How the White Tract became the centre of a development disputeThe White Tract is a 229-acre property in the Town of Awendaw, bordering the Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge. The land was controlled by Pulte Home Company and became the subject of conservation concerns after development plans received approvals in 2006. The development proposal envisioned approximately 208 single-family homes on 182 acres of the property. Although some permits and approvals had been secured, conservation advocates argued that a development of this scale could damage an ecologically important area.The proposed homes were expected to rely on septic systems, which became a major point of disagreement. Conservationists warned that wastewater from the systems could affect groundwater quality and surrounding waterways. They also raised concerns about the consequences of placing dense residential development so close to protected wildlife habitat.The Coastal Conservation League, Friends of Coastal South Carolina and Charleston Waterkeeper opposed the proposal and worked with SCELP to challenge permits and approvals associated with the project. Their efforts continued through years of legal proceedings and public advocacy.Why conservation groups wanted the land protectedThe White Tract's location makes it important to the wider Cape Romain ecosystem. The neighbouring national wildlife refuge contains marshes, beaches and barrier islands that support migratory birds, sea turtles and other wildlife. According to the conservation organisations, Cape Romain provides important habitat and feeding grounds for federally threatened migratory birds. It is also home to more sea turtle nests than anywhere else in South Carolina. The area plays an important role beyond wildlife protection. Its marshes help filter water, support coastal fisheries and provide natural protection against storms and flooding.Grace Gasper, executive director of Friends of Coastal South Carolina, described the property as a place of global ecological significance. She highlighted its importance as a stopover for birds migrating between South America and the Arctic, as well as its role in supporting wintering waterfowl and sea turtle nesting. Conservation advocates argued that protecting the refuge's existing boundaries would not be enough if neighbouring land remained vulnerable to intensive development. Preserving the White Tract would help maintain a wider natural landscape and reduce the pressure of construction near sensitive habitats.How the settlement makes permanent conservation possibleThe breakthrough came after the Open Space Institute identified a potential funding source for purchasing the property. Pulte then participated in discussions with the institute, SCELP and the conservation organisations to develop an agreement. Under the settlement, Pulte has agreed to sell the entire White Tract to the Open Space Institute for permanent conservation protection. The institute will acquire the land, with the possibility of its future incorporation into the Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge.The agreement also provides for SCELP to dismiss the pending legal challenges once the property is permanently conserved. The settlement represents a change from the earlier adversarial dispute, with the developer and conservation groups working together towards a shared outcome. SCELP senior managing attorney Leslie Lenhardt described the agreement as an example of how parties can move beyond opposing positions to achieve a conservation result.Pulte also agreed to introduce additional environmental enhancements at its Farms at Longleaf community in Hollywood, Charleston County, and the Rock Six community in Dorchester County. These measures are intended to provide further consideration for water quality, wildlife habitat and community health.What happens next for the White TractThe parties have yet to announce an official closing date for the transaction. Until the transaction is completed, the proposed transfer to the Open Space Institute remains an upcoming step rather than a completed acquisition. The conservation groups have welcomed the outcome as a significant achievement after two decades of community advocacy. They have also acknowledged support from state and local leaders, including Governor Henry McMaster, the South Carolina Office of Resilience, the Town of Awendaw and Charleston and Dorchester counties.The agreement is important for more than the future of one property. It demonstrates how conservation organisations, public agencies and private developers can work together to protect environmentally sensitive land while allowing development in more suitable locations.For the White Tract, a property once considered for hundreds of homes, the proposed sale offers a different future: permanent protection of its natural landscape alongside one of South Carolina's important coastal wildlife refuges.

articles.title: X-energy gets green light to build its first small modular nuclear reactors | TechCrunch
articles.summary: X-energy received a construction permit from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission to build four reactors in Texas.
articles.body:
Nuclear startup X-energy announced Monday that it had been given the go-ahead from federal officials to build its first four commercial reactors.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved the construction permit application for four of X-energy’s Xe-100 reactors at a Dow chemical plant in Texas. Each reactor will be capable of generating 80 megawatts of electricity and 200 megawatts of heat. X-energy says the approval is the first for an advanced nuclear reactor at an industrial site in the United States.

The U.S. nuclear industry has pinned its hopes on small modular reactors — or SMRs — like those being developed by X-energy. By shrinking the reactor, proponents say it will speed construction and reduce costs, though those advantages have yet to be proven. No SMR is currently in operation in the U.S., and X-energy says Dow’s reactors won’t be operational until the early 2030s.

X-energy claims that its reactor design, which flows helium gas over uranium-containing fuel pellets, is safer than many existing reactors, but the Union of Concerned Scientists questioned the claim and the speed with which X-energy received the permit.

“The NRC only accomplished this feat by pushing consideration of critical safety questions to a later date—issues the NRC should’ve fully resolved before green lighting construction,” Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety for the organization, said in a statement.

The nuclear industry has benefitted from strong interest from hyperscalers and data center developers, who are desperate for any and all sources of electricity. Amazon’s Climate Pledge Fund led X-energy’s $500 million Series C-1 , and the big tech company has also committed to buying 5 gigawatts of capacity from the nuclear startup.

X-energy rode that wave of excitement earlier this year when its April initial public offering raised $1 billion. But since then, investors’ optimism has tempered.

The hesitancy isn’t surprising: Nuclear power plants are expensive to build and can take years to complete. Eventually, X-energy hopes to rein in both time and cost, but its first reactors are likely to be pricey.

The new permit approval gave X-energy a small jolt yesterday, though it was only enough to recover last week’s losses. The company’s shares are trading at less than half their initial offering price.

articles.title: ‘Everything and everyone we love is at stake’: Thunberg slams COP31 talks
articles.summary: Climate activist urges world leaders to put people and planet before profit as she arrives at UN climate talks.
articles.body:
Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has condemned the United Nations climate talks as hypocritical and urged world leaders to put people and planet ahead of profits and power.

Thunberg made the comments on Tuesday as she arrived at the COP31 conference in the Turkish resort city of Antalya .

“It’s a hypocrisy every year that the host countries are given an opportunity to whitewash themselves and we know that these negotiations are filled with lobbyists, paid by the very destructive industries which are benefiting from our extremely violent status quo,” Thunberg said.

“Our political and economic systems that have become incompatible with human nature.”

The talks follow a year of deadly climate-related disasters, including heatwaves and floods, and another energy shock caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.

COP31 co-hosts Turkiye and Australia are promoting renewable energy and rooftop solar installations, but both still rely heavily on fossil fuels, especially coal, to generate electricity. Previous hosts, including Brazil, the United Arab Emirates and Azerbaijan, are major oil producers.

Climate change is “threatening everything”, Thunberg said, warning that “everything and everyone we love is at stake”.

“We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she said.

Thunberg rose to prominence in 2018 as a 15-year-old, when she began a solitary “School Strike for Climate” outside the Swedish parliament.

The Antalya summit is the first she has attended since the 2021 talks in Glasgow, Scotland, where she dismissed world leaders’ promises as “blah, blah, blah”.

She has also c ampaigned for other causes , including the Free Palestine movement, and more recently backed French students protesting for more school resources.

Her arrival in Antalya has created excitement among many of the youth climate activists at COP31 who are demanding more climate finance.

“I hope that Greta’s presence here reminds us of why we started this work in the first place: to push for meaningful change, hold decision-makers accountable, and work towards a better future for all of humanity,” Amber Turner, a 26-year-old fellow with the Alliance of Small Island States, told The Associated Press news agency.

Qiyun Woo, a youth environmentalist from Singapore, said Thunberg’s “powerful” presence “adds to calls from a generation that inherits the consequences of these negotiations”.

COP31 runs in Antalya until November 20.

Next year’s edition, COP32, is scheduled to take place in Ethiopia’s capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.
